items.title: Beyond Driver Monitoring: A Systems Approach to Understanding Lifecycle Risks of AI-Based Driver Behaviour Monitoring Systems
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence-based Driver Behaviour Monitoring Systems (AI-DBMS) are used in heavy vehicle fleets to detect unsafe driving states and behaviours such as fatigue and distraction. However, limited research has examined risks across their lifecycle. This study used Hierarchical Task Analysis (HTA) to identify risks associated with AI-DBMS implementation. An HTA model of the AI-DBMS lifecycle was developed and validated through interviews with technology developers, fleet operators, regulators, and researchers. Participants selected HTA sub-goals relevant to their expertise and discussed risks and controls. Five risk categories were identified: (i) technology and system design, (ii) data-related, (iii) governance and regulatory, (iv) organisational, and (v) human and behavioural. Four control categories were identified: (i) governance and organisational, (ii) human-centred design and implementation, (iii) system assurance, and (iv) data management. Findings show AI-DBMS risks extend beyond technical performance and the driver-technology interface, highlighting the need for coordinated Human Factors approaches across the AI-DBMS lifecycle.

items.title: Beyond Knowledge Transfer: Non-Human Embodiment for Environmental Education
items.abstract: Effective conservation education must communicate ecological facts while also making distant environmental threats personally meaningful. Virtual reality (VR) may support this goal by allowing learners to experience such threats from a non-human perspective, yet it remains unclear whether embodied interactive VR primarily improves factual learning, affective engagement, or both. We present EcoShift VR, a dual-ecosystem experience in which users embody either a Sunda pangolin facing pollution and poaching or a blue shark facing pollution and bycatch. We evaluated EcoShift VR in a controlled 2 × 2 between-subjects study (N = 40) comparing Medium (embodied interactive VR vs. lecture-style informational video) and Ecosystem (terrestrial vs. marine). As the media differed jointly in immersion, embodiment, agency, and interaction, their individual contributions cannot be isolated. All four conditions showed significant within-group factual knowledge gains after Holm–Bonferroni correction across the four paired comparisons, with no significant Medium effect on knowledge gain. Before multiplicity correction, 10 of the 13 Medium effects were statistically significant and favored embodied interactive VR, including nature connectedness, state empathy, perceived environmental awareness, and several curiosity and inquisitiveness measures. After Holm–Bonferroni adjustment across the 13 Medium comparisons, only the three state-empathy subscales (affective, cognitive, and associative) and the post-experience domain-specific curiosity composite remained statistically significant. A secondary within-condition analysis also identified a significant increase in nature connectedness for VR–Marine (p Holm =.0053), although the overall Medium effect on nature connectedness did not survive correction. Other initially significant Medium effects were similarly attenuated after adjustment, while environmental-attitude gains remained directionally favorable to VR but inconclusive. These findings suggest that the broader embodied interactive VR experience can complement conventional environmental education, particularly by supporting empathy and conservation-oriented curiosity alongside factual learning.

items.title: Beyond Model Choice: Designing Maintainable and Source-Grounded LLM Assistants for Academic Advising
items.abstract: Students increasingly rely on Large Language Models (LLMs) for academic advice, yet general-purpose models often lack institution-specific knowledge and can provide confident but inaccurate guidance. This creates risks for students and raises design questions about how universities should develop reliable, accountable, and maintainable LLM advising systems. This study evaluates three approaches for incorporating institutional knowledge into LLM-based advising systems: prompting, retrieval, and fine-tuning, compared across three open-weight models producing 48 configurations. Evaluation used an LLM-as-judge framework validated by student advisors serving as domain experts. Results show that the system prompt has the greatest impact on response quality, while retrieval provides complementary gains through source attribution. Fine-tuning produces only modest improvements. The LLM judge closely mirrors expert rankings, though it consistently assigns higher scores. These findings shift attention from model performance alone to the design and governance of maintainable, source-visible, uncertainty-aware advising systems embedded within human-led academic advising practice.

items.title: Beyond Resume Keywords: Eliminating Entry-Level Burnout Through AI-Driven Workplace Culture Matching
items.abstract: Entry-level hiring in emerging startup ecosystems suffers from a critical structural flaw: an over-reliance on superficial resume keyword matching at the expense of workplace culture compatibility. Drawing on industry workforce data and qualitative insights synthesized from over 50 structured interviews with Chief Human Resources Officers (CHROs) and startup founders on the career podcast "Let’s Hear It From...", this paper examines the root causes of early-career attrition and Gen-Z workplace burnout. Industry benchmarks indicate that early-stage companies face a 43.7% rookie attrition rate—incurring ₹1.5 lakh to ₹3 lakh per bad hire—while 47.5% of startup employees report low psychological well-being. Qualitative findings reveal five recurring failure points among fresh graduates: mindset misalignment, inadequate organizational research, AI-assisted interview façades, theoretical baggage paired with low learning agility, and workplace etiquette deficits. To address this misalignment, this paper introduces the Human Energy Matching Framework, an automated, cognitive AI-driven methodology deployed via AlignCulture. By cross-referencing unstructured executive cultural baselines with multidimensional candidate behavioral assessments across dimensions such as Values Alignment, Learning Agility, Work Style Fit, and Purpose Alignment, organizations and higher education placement cells can transition from reactive keyword filtering to sustainable, wellness-driven talent integration. Author’s Note: Generative AI tools were utilized to assist in synthesizing qualitative transcripts from the "Let's Hear It From..." podcast archive and structuring the manuscript. All conceptual frameworks, empirical observations, and conclusions are the sole work of the author.

items.title: Boundaries for generative AI use and task delegation in nursing education: a scoping review with critical evidence synthesis
items.abstract: Introduction Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used in nursing education, but studies rarely evaluate task delegation explicitly. This review mapped evidence on educational tasks, contexts of use, and safeguards to inform boundaries for using large language models (LLMs) and delegating educational tasks. Methods This scoping review with critical evidence synthesis used JBI guidance for evidence mapping and PRISMA-ScR for reporting. MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched through 7 August 2026 for studies involving direct interaction between prelicensure nursing students and LLM-based systems. The review team extracted outcomes, risks, safeguards, and human oversight. The team proposed delegation statuses by considering the consequences of error, error detectability under specified safeguards, the need for human judgment, confidence in the evidence, and oversight feasibility. Results Of the 440 records screened, 46 studies comprising 47 educational application profiles were included. Of the 146 outcome records, 115 were favorable, 13 were mixed, 10 showed no difference, 6 were unfavorable, and 2 were unclear. Twelve studies (26.1%) reported at least one objectively verified error or event or an adverse educational outcome. Among the 118 safeguards, 100 (84.7%) were proposed or implemented without evaluation beyond implementation, five (4.2%) were evaluated for feasibility or acceptability, and 13 (11.0%) were evaluated for risk reduction. The proposed matrix comprises 16 task categories: eight conditionally delegable, five restricted to a supportive role, two unsuitable for automated delegation, and one with insufficient evidence. Conclusion The matrix offers a preliminary framework for task-specific decisions. Bounded knowledge support and low-risk formative feedback may be conditionally delegable with appropriate safeguards and oversight. AI should support clinical reasoning and care planning, whereas final grading, competence decisions, and ethical judgment should remain human responsibilities. The matrix requires validation and updating as direct evidence, particularly on safeguard effectiveness, becomes available. Clinical trial number Not applicable.

items.title: Byte-Sized AI Learning: Lessons Learned after Building AI Literacy MLIS Learning Content
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is renowned for its stochastic nature, where powerful computational performance is jeopardized by inconsistent, vague, and even flawed reasoning. When it comes to teaching MLIS students about serving information needs, seeking, use, and literacy, AI curricula present both opportunities and limitations to successful instruction. A research team explored a critical curriculum that draws distinctly from LIS examples of search trends, AI hallucination, and scholarly risks. Rather than a fixed and performance-based curriculum, this learning material aimed to bring MLIS students into conversations on AI use, risks, and even refusal. This work-in-progress study, which centers on student agency, contemplation, and critique, offers preliminary findings and opportunities for idea exchanges among LIS faculty.

items.title: Calibration-Free Eye Tracking through Binocular-Constrained Homography Normalization
items.abstract: Implicit user calibration and calibration-free eye-tracking methods have been explored to improve the usability of gaze-based interactions. However, these methods for regression- and model-based approaches typically require multiple observations or camera-display calibration. Therefore, we propose a binocular-constrained homography normalization method that enables calibration-free gaze estimation from a single observation without camera-display calibration. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first homography-based framework to incorporate calibration-free gaze estimation. For each eye, the corneal center and optical axis are estimated using a 3D eyeball model with a monocular camera, and the point-of-gaze is computed using homography transformations derived from both eyes. The proposed method achieved a mean horizontal angular error of 1.01° under the tested conditions. The experimental evaluations supported the feasibility of the proposed method and identified directions for further improvement.

items.title: Can AI Make with Us? Exploring Tacit Knowledge and Emotion in AI-Supported Making
items.abstract: As AI reshapes how people learn and create, questions arise about forms of knowledge that are embodied, practice-based, and difficult to articulate. This study examines how learners physically co-create with AI and what forms of tacit knowledge emerge through that process. It further investigates how emotions surface and are managed throughout AI-supported making. Through this examination, this study aims to holistically capture the cognitive, emotional, and behavioral dimensions of tacit knowledge acquisition in an AI-supported making environment. We designed and facilitated a pilot workshop centered on e-textile making with community members in Champaign-Urbana, Illinois in April 2026. E-textile was selected for its inherently tactile and embodied nature, offering a deliberate contrast to AI’s text-based, formalized mode of knowledge. Nine participants engaged freely with AI tools of their choice alongside human facilitators, creating a naturalistic environment where both forms of support coexisted. To capture the holistic process of cognition, behavioral patterns, and emotional responses, think-aloud protocols, observation, pre-post surveys, and interviews were used as data collection methods. Preliminary findings reveal no consensus on how AI supported ideation, process, or outcomes, suggesting that its role in tacit-knowledge-rich making is highly individual. Emotionally, participants expressed confidence, curiosity, and surprise throughout the workshops, while also navigating moments of stress and frustration. This study contributes to Library and Information Science understanding of how human-AI collaboration unfolds in spaces where knowledge is socially constructed and physically embodied. It further offers insight into the emotional experiences that emerge and are managed throughout AI-supported learning.

items.title: Can AI Personalise Meaningfulness? Bodies, Prediction, and Postdigital Health and Physical Education
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly woven into Health and Physical Education (HPE) through motion analysis, wearable data, adaptive task design, automated feedback, and generative support for teachers. These developments are often associated with personalisation and, by extension, with the possibility of making learning more meaningful for individual students. This conceptual article questions that connection. Drawing on Kretchmar’s philosophy of meaning in movement, Meaningful Physical Education (MPE), and postdigital accounts of entangled pedagogy and technological mediation, it argues that meaningfulness is not a personalised output but a postdigital accomplishment. It emerges through embodied activity, relationships, material settings, cultural practices, interpretation, and time. Particular AI-supported arrangements may expand or constrain these conditions, but no technical adjustment can guarantee what an experience will come to mean. The analysis develops four tensions: personal relevance between dialogue and prediction; challenge between embodied negotiation and adaptive optimisation; fun, sociality, and delight beyond engagement analytics; and biographical meaning in relation to computational memory. It shows how personalised systems can also influence whose movements, preferences, and histories become visible and valued. The article concludes with five commitments for keeping meaningfulness open in postdigital HPE: interpretive openness, negotiated personalisation, embodied and relational attentiveness, collective possibility, and temporal and infrastructural humility.

items.title: CENTRY: A Probabilistic Latent-State Model for Continual AI Risk Estimation, Monitoring, and Regulation
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems are increasingly deployed in safety-critical applications, yet existing AI safety frameworks primarily define, categorize, or govern AI risk rather than proposing implementable models and methods for continually estimating, monitoring, and regulating risk throughout an AI system's operational lifetime. This paper proposes CENTRY, a probabilistic framework that enables continual risk estimation, monitoring, and regulation of a deployed AI system from its interactions with its environment. The framework models AI risk as arising from three intrinsic sources: datasets, hardware resources, and models/algorithms. A structured latent-variable model is developed in which the latent representation is decomposed into a fast interaction subspace that captures the evolving AI--environment dynamics and three slow latent subspaces that encode the long-term risk states associated with the dataset, hardware, and model components. Rather than requiring a ground-truth risk label at every time step, the component-risk states are treated as latent variables and are learned by maximizing a variational evidence lower bound, optionally informed during training and continual refinement by evidence-supported behavior--cause records. The resulting framework unifies continual probabilistic inference, online risk estimation, and adaptive risk regulation in an implementable architecture. Under the explicit assumptions stated for the corresponding results, we establish formal guarantees spanning safety, learning, inference, and operations, including finite-horizon and asymptotic risk-budget compliance, regret and convergence bounds for adaptive regulation, consistency and identifiability of component-risk ratings, and detection-delay, false-alarm, containment, and computational-complexity characterizations.

items.title: ChildAI-Gov: An Evidence-Linked AI System for Assessing EdTech Policies Against Children's Digital Rights
items.abstract: We present ChildAI-Gov, an explainable AI system for assessing whether education-technology (EdTech) policies respect children's digital rights. Generative AI is reaching children's education faster than its governance can keep pace, yet checking a tool against children's rights remains manual, expert-dependent, and slow. We propose the Child Rights Impact Score (CRIS), an evidence-linked measure across five dimensions: safety, privacy, transparency, autonomy, and non-discrimination. ChildAI-Gov reads an EdTech tool's privacy or AI policy and scores each dimension by combining a large-language-model judgement (gpt-4o-mini) with a deterministic rule check. A retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) component grounds every score in the governing provisions, retrieved from a curated knowledge base of children's rights frameworks (the EU AI Act, UNICEF guidance, and others), so each score is tied to the evidence behind it and an auditor can trace which provision it rests on. We also construct AIPolicy-EdTech, a dataset of 57 real EdTech policies. On it, the five dimensions cohered as a single measure (Cronbach's alpha = 0.79), and grounding made scoring stricter while preserving rankings; an ungrounded baseline was far more lenient, passing nearly half the policies where ChildAI-Gov passed none. It offers evidence-linked decision support on documented commitments, not observation of real-world behaviour or determinations of legal compliance.

items.title: Clinical AI agents: a short narrative review
items.abstract: Clinical artificial intelligence (AI) agents represent an emerging generation of AI systems. They extend conventional clinical decision support through goal-directed planning, tool interaction and adaptation of actions to intermediate results. Memory may support these functions but is not essential in every implementation. Human oversight is a safeguard for clinical deployment rather than an intrinsic capability. This short narrative review summarizes current evidence regarding the core architectural features, representative clinical applications, and primary implementation challenges of clinical AI agents. Recent studies indicate promising applications in diagnostic decision support, workflow automation, patient communication, and evidence synthesis. However, existing evidence remains largely based on technical validation studies, proof-of-concept systems, and conceptual frameworks, with relatively limited prospective evaluation in routine clinical practice. Key challenges include establishing reliable evaluation frameworks, ensuring process-level safety, developing effective governance structures, and generating robust clinical evidence to support implementation. Although technological progress is rapid, widespread adoption will require not only further technical advances but also rigorous clinical validation, transparent governance, and successful integration into healthcare workflows. Clinical AI agents may become useful components of multidisciplinary healthcare workflows, provided that future research addresses the remaining methodological and implementation challenges.

items.title: Cluster-Based Learner Profiling in AI-Supported Educational Contexts: Evidence from Junior High School Students
items.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly embedded in educational settings, learner heterogeneity can no longer be adequately described through single-variable comparisons. This study identifies learner profiles in AI-supported educational contexts using three theoretically grounded feature dimensions: AI self-efficacy, digital literacy, and cross-disciplinary integration self-efficacy. These dimensions were operationalized using eight indicators reflecting students’ AI-related confidence, digital information-processing competence, and integrative learning readiness. Based on 8,022 valid responses from eighth-grade students in the collaborative database of the Taiwan Assessment of Student Achievement: Longitudinal Study and the Taiwan i-Generation Panel Study, available from the Survey Research Data Archive, Academia Sinica, all input indicators were normalized using Z -score scaling to construct a standardized feature space for distance estimation. A two-stage clustering procedure was adopted. First, two-step cluster analysis was performed to compare candidate solutions based on Akaike Information Criterion and Bayesian Information Criterion values; subsequently, K -means clustering was conducted with the number of clusters fixed at six to estimate the final learner profiles. The results supported six profiles: high-scoring integrated; very low-scoring; AI-moderate, digitally weak; broadly below-average; digitally adequate, AI-integration weak; and near-average balanced. The profiles showed that learner heterogeneity was not organized along a simple high–low continuum but appeared as asymmetric configurations within the multidimensional feature space. Post-clustering analyses further showed that digital-literacy indicators and AI evaluation had the largest descriptive between-profile separations, and that cluster membership differed significantly by gender. The findings extend AI literacy research from average-based comparisons to cluster-based learner profiling and provide a basis for differentiated educational support and data-driven decision-making in AI-related educational settings.

items.title: Co-Defining Transparency for Clinical AI: A Replicable Participatory Methodology
items.abstract: Transparency is the most invoked safeguard for clinical AI, yet frameworks (e.g. the EU AI Act, FUTURE-AI) are specified top-down by regulators and technical experts, not bottom-up by the frontline users whose trust and adoption they should calibrate. This disconnect exacerbates the central deployment failure of clinical AI, miscalibrated reliance and adoption (such as automation bias, deskilling, or disuse), which technical explanation alone does not resolve. We argue that "how much transparency, of what kind, and for whom" is an empirical, context-dependent question, and present a replicable participatory methodology to answer it, instantiated at a large European university hospital. A cumulative chain of six workshops engages an inter-professional panel (clinicians, patient and caregiver partners, students) in agnostic, open-ended elicitation: 274 stakeholder verbatims and external benchmarks (eCH-0272, EU AI Act, Stanford FMTI) yield 20 indicators (18 prioritised and 2 recovered at a later stage), rated across five clinical scenarios of graduated intervention before and after technical briefings, discussed with legal experts, and translated into concrete implementation features. As an existence proof, the use case yields decision-useful signals: human review of automated decisions is the single most critical transparency indicator (84% of participants), and required transparency for adoption rises monotonically with the perceived risk of intervention, corroborating WHO risk-proportionality. A short explainability briefing did not substantially shift participants' transparency requirements. Of 151 evaluated AI transparency solutions, 79 were accepted as-is, covering (at least partially) 17 out of the 20 selected indicators. We position the six-workshop protocol (not its single-site outcomes) as the transferable artefact and release all instruments to support replication.

items.title: Co-Thinker or Cognitive Crutch? A Systematic Review of Human-AI Collaboration in Mathematics
items.abstract: A study of the relationship between AI and self-regulated learning (SRL) in university-level mathematics education is conducted. The aim is to determine if AI is a good tool for learning and whether students can take better care of it or if it is simply a tool for students to be so dependent on external support. Consistent with the PRISMA 2020 guidelines, we review 35 empirical studies published between 2023 and 2026. Our selected studies were obtained using Scopus, Web of Science, and the national databases with a specific focus on undergraduate mathematics education. The data were analyzed thematically based on the types of AI used, Zimmerman's three SRL phases, students' epistemic autonomy, and mathematical reasoning results. The results show that 60% of the reviewed experimental studies used AI as an exploratory partner with structured Socratic prompting, while 25.7% applied adaptive scaffolding and 14.3% resulted in significant cognitive offloading. The review also found a lack of balance in the use of SRL dimensions. Roughly 80% of interventions were focused on real-time task completion, whereas less attention was given to forethought and critical self-reflection. Overall, the findings indicate that the impact of AI on learning depends on how well it is implemented. Using AI unsupervised, but without guidance, is prone to creating a false sense of deep understanding while weakening students' ability to solve problems independently. Instead, structured collaborative prompting gives students more control over their thinking and therefore enhances their ability to understand the relationship between abstract concepts and helps them to have a stronger sense of deductive reasoning and evidence

items.title: Collaboration to Constraint: Rethinking Generative Artificial Intelligence in User Experience & Interface Design
items.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) tools have become a standard in the User Experience (UX) & User Interface (UI) design workflows. There has been a shift in Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems reshaping how designers ideate, research, generate layouts, and refine interfaces. These AI systems promise speed and creativity within the UX workflows, but the increase in AI integration has raised questions around control and autonomy shift when they are used for design generation. In this thesis I have investigated the design outcomes when AI is positioned as a creative collaborator, influencing the decision authority and cognitive ownership. In this study, I have used research-through-design combining with auto-ethnography reflections, comparative user interface generation experiments (including Lovable AI-based website creations), and participatory engagements like Open Studio activity and a co-design workshop. The findings suggested that introducing AI early in the design process can lead the design to a specific framework, hierarchy and interaction pattern that narrow divergence. Designers can experience a drift in cognitive ownership while retaining their decision authority when authorship is distributed across prompts, iterations, and AI-generated drafts. In my experiments, AI outputs were polished and plausible but converged towards a similar structural layout. It reflected the influence of dominant pattern in their training data. This thesis argues for responsible integration of AI through careful timing, clear override options, and tools that make AI-driven influence visible, instead of rejecting it completely.

items.title: CoMotion: A Real-Time System for User-Driven Semantic Steering in Text-to-Motion Generation
items.abstract: Current text-to-motion frameworks typically operate as a rigid, one-shot workflow where users are unable to intervene during the generation process, effectively limiting all refinement efforts to the iterative modification of the text prompt. This black-box process hinders iterative design, leading to inefficiency. Furthermore, natural language inherently suffers from ambiguity when describing fine-grained 3D motions, making it difficult for users to articulate their intent solely through text precisely. In this paper, we propose CoMotion, a real-time system that shifts the interaction paradigm from static text prompting to user-driven semantic steering. Instead of requiring users to restart the entire generation process for every modification, CoMotion operates directly within a discrete latent space by retrieving prompt-relevant atomic actions and presenting them as user-visible, adjustable controls. Through CoMotion, users can adjust semantic steering levels for these atomic actions to guide the generation toward their intent without the computational overhead of full text-to-motion model re-inference. Our approach provides a more diverse design pathway for the traditional one-shot text-to-motion generation process, enabling fine-grained, personalized motion control during generation. We validate our system using a standardized benchmark based on Large Language Models. Quantitative experiments demonstrate that CoMotion enables robust semantic correction and geometric diversity while maintaining the kinematic quality of the generated motions. Crucially, by transforming complex generative tasks into low-latency, interactive operations, CoMotion supports an interactive refinement workflow for the evaluated motion generation tasks.

items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is intensifying longstanding questions about the purposes of higher education, the authority of human judgment, and the university's obligations to society. This conceptual, theory-building article argues that AI competence is educationally insufficient when learners lack institutional conditions that make judgment consequential. Drawing on AI-literacy scholarship, ecological theories of agency, democratic education, the capabilities approach, and critical educational technology, it develops an ecological framework of Consequential Human Agency. The framework distinguishes individual capability from agency achieved in interaction with institutional authority, rights to contest and appeal, accountability, and material conditions of participation. Ethical, civic, professional, and leadership agency are treated as contexts of enactment rather than stages or measurable competencies. The article argues that universities are not benign guarantors of agency: as purchasers of platforms, assessment authorities, and users of surveillance and analytics, they can enable or constrain it. Higher education should therefore cultivate judgment while establishing institutional rights and procedures through which students and faculty can question, override, appeal, and help govern consequential AI-mediated decisions.

items.title: Continuing Education as Ethical Infrastructure: Informal AI Learning in Academic Librarianship
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming academic librarianship, requiring sustained ethical, evaluative, and instructional learning. Drawing on interviews with fourteen U.S. STEM academic librarians and scholarship on AI literacy and professional development, this paper examines how librarians develop AI competence through experimentation, peer networks, and personal knowledge management amid uneven institutional support. These conditions shift the costs of adaptation onto individual practitioners and raise concerns about equity, labor, and sustainability. The paper reframes continuing education as sociotechnical infrastructure for AI learning, identifies informal learning as structurally compelled labor, and proposes a role for library and information science (LIS) educators in designing ethical, collaborative, and sustained professional learning. Practice-based pathways, communities of practice, protected learning time, and institutional governance can support critical judgment as AI systems change.

items.title: CRAFTMANSHIP AS A CATEGORY IN THE PHILOSOPHY OF ART OF THE DIGITAL AGE: A PHENOMENOLOGICAL APPROACH
items.abstract: This article offers a philosophical reconstruction of the criteria for artistic mastery in the context of the proliferation of digital media and generative artificial intelligence. It challenges the tendency to equate mastery solely with technical proficiency, professional status, or the visual perfection of a work, while conversely reducing amateurism merely to aesthetic inferiority. The methodology integrates a phenomenological analysis of aesthetic experience, the hermeneutics of artistic decision-making, a media-philosophical perspective, and a critical examination of contemporary literature on the philosophy of AI. It is argued that generative technology alters not only the artist’s toolkit but also the modes of form emergence, the distribution of agency, and the processes of perception. The study proposes distinguishing between image generation, its artistic articulation, and the aesthetic event, processes that do not necessarily coincide. The novelty of this research lies in delineating three levels of an artistic work-technical generation, authorial articulation, and the aesthetic event and in conceptualizing mastery as a reflexively responsible capacity to organize the relationships between these levels, rather than as a mere sum of skills or a property of a finished artifact. Conclusions. Based on this, a multidimensional model of mastery is developed, encompassing intentionality, media literacy, reflexive selection, temporal depth, the productivity of aesthetic experience, and responsibility. It is demonstrated that the «human versus machine» dichotomy is less analytically productive than the distinction between the automated reproduction of the recognizable and responsible form-creation. Amateurism is interpreted as an open mode of participation in culture—one capable of evolving into mastery, independent of commercial or institutional legitimation.

items.title: Creating meaning at work or providing career support? How servant leaders enhance followers’ vocational outcomes
items.abstract: Do servant leaders shape their followers’ vocational outcomes by the career support they provide or by helping followers find meaning at work? Drawing on self-determination theory, we test these two accounts, examining their competing effects on followers’ thriving at work, career satisfaction, and job search behaviors. Using the critical incident method (Study 1), we found that servant leaders influence vocational outcomes by deepening followers’ meaning at work, but not by providing career support. In a four-wave study (Study 2), both pathways were significant. A field study (Study 3) again supported only the meaning at work pathway, showing that meaning at work was most salient for followers with lower levels of work volition. An internal meta-analysis confirmed that both pathways carry a positive indirect effect in aggregate, but that the pathway through meaning at work is significantly stronger. Taken together, our results indicate that servant leadership is more vocationally consequential through the meaning followers internalize than the career support they receive, particularly among followers whose vocational agency is more constrained.

items.title: Designing AI at the Rural Edge: A Micro-Social Venture Framework for Community-Led Digital Innovation
items.abstract: Generative and other AI-enabled technologies are accessible to small organisations, yet human–AI interaction (HAI) design guidance focuses on relatively direct user–system interaction. Rural HCI, community-centred design, participatory AI, digital inclusion, and social-enterprise research show that AI use is socially and organisationally situated. This late-breaking work develops the Micro-Social Venture (MSV) Framework through integrative conceptual synthesis of 55 selected sources. The framework connects six dimensions: Place, Community Agency, Organisational Mediation, Digital and AI Capability, Resource Conditions, and Governance and Social Outcomes. Its distinctive contribution is to treat the social venture as part of HAI itself: a community-embedded socio-technical intermediary through which AI is encountered, adapted, governed, and potentially refused. Five design propositions address place, collective agency, resource asymmetry, negotiated trust, and community stewardship. The framework is generative rather than predictive, offering HCI a diagnostic lens for examining community-embedded AI at geographic, organisational, infrastructural, and participatory edges.

items.title: DESIGNING AI-RESISTANT TASKS AS A TOOL FOR ASSESSING THE ANALYTICAL AND CRITICAL COMPETENCIES OF FUTURE TEACHERS
items.abstract: This article provides a theoretical foundation for assessing the analytical and critical competencies of future teachers in the era of generative artificial intelligence. It has been demonstrated that the limited reliability of automated AI-detection tools necessitates a shift from evaluating the final written product to a "process-over-product" diagnostic paradigm, while upholding the principles of academic integrity. Within the structure of an educator's analytical - critical competencies, the cognitive-diagnostic, didactic-design and reflexive-metacognitive components have been distinguished. A didactic model has been developed for designing AI - resistant assignments that focus on higher-order thinking skills, specifically "Analyzing", "Evaluating" and ″Creating″ according to Bloom's Taxonomy. The model incorporates the ″Three Zones ″ framework and utilizes three diagnostic formats: the analysis of contradictory pedagogical cases (Case Study), the cognitive auditing of AI-generated content (Reverse Engineering), and in-person, dialogue-based defense using the Socratic method (Socratic Defense). Furthermore, a criterion - based, multi-level rubric has been proposed comprising verification-analytical, didactic-adaptive, and metacognitive-authorial criteria to objectively assess students' professional agency and critical thinking.

items.title: Determinants of job pressure among physical education lecturers in higher education: evidence from Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam
items.abstract: This study investigates the determinants of job pressure among physical education lecturers in higher education institutions in Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam, within the context of increasing academic demands and postpandemic transformations. Despite the growing importance of occupational stress in academia, limited research has focused specifically on physical education lecturers, particularly in developing countries. A quantitative research design was employed, with data collected from 220 physical education lecturers using a structured questionnaire. Reliability analysis (Cronbach’s alpha), exploratory factor analysis (EFA), and multiple regression analysis were performed using SPSS 20.0 to examine the relationships between the variables. The results indicate that job pressure is significantly influenced by five key factors, namely, the working environment (β = 0.760, p < 0.001), workload (β = 0.136, p < 0.001), role ambiguity (β = 0.096, p = 0.006), job performance (β = 0.091, p = 0.013), and workplace relationships (β = 0.075, p = 0.027). Among these, the working environment has the strongest effect, highlighting the critical role of organizational and environmental conditions in shaping job pressure. These findings contribute to the literature by confirming the multidimensional nature of job pressure and extending the application of person–environment fit theory, role theory, and transactional theory in the context of higher education in developing countries. Furthermore, the study provides empirical evidence from Vietnam, addressing a significant research gap. Practically, the results of this study suggest that universities should prioritize improving working conditions, optimizing workload distribution, and clarifying job roles to reduce job pressure and enhance lecturer performance. These implications are particularly relevant for institutions undergoing rapid transformation and quality assurance processes.

items.title: Determinants of Mechanical Ventilator Adoption in Healthcare Emergency Settings
items.abstract: Mechanical ventilation (MV) is the recommended standard of care in many emergencies, yet its adoption by nursing professionals remains inconsistent. This research examines whether perceived clinical expertise is associated with emergency nurses' intention to use MV, directly and indirectly through trust in MV technology and attitude toward MV, and whether emergency severity moderates these associations. Emergency nurses (N = 236) were randomly assigned to one of four vignettes of decreasing acuity: cardiorespiratory arrest, severe hypoxaemia, chest trauma with respiratory compromise, and acute pulmonary oedema. Structural equation modelling showed that expertise was associated with trust and intention, trust with attitude, and attitude with intention; the serial indirect effect of expertise on intention through trust and attitude was significant. Because these constructs were measured concurrently, this effect is interpreted as an indirect association rather than as evidence of causal transmission. Higher severity strengthened the direct association between expertise and intention and weakened the association between trust and attitude, so that the serial indirect association declined as acuity increased. These findings are consistent with a shift from deliberative to automatic processing under time pressure and suggest that training should build expertise to automaticity for maximum-acuity scenarios while fostering trust in lower-acuity ones.

items.title: Digital Health Innovations and Well-Being of the Aged Population: A Theoretical Approach
items.abstract: Digital health innovations are increasingly reshaping the delivery of healthcare and creating new possibilities for supporting the well-being of ageing populations. From telemedicine and remote patient monitoring to mobile health applications, wearable devices, and artificial intelligence-enabled services, these technologies can improve access to healthcare, strengthen disease management, and promote greater independence among older adults. However, their implications for the well-being of the aged population extend beyond clinical outcomes and involve psychological, social, behavioral, and functional dimensions of ageing. The paper adopted a secondary source of data. This theoretical study examines the relationship between digital health innovations and the well-being of older adults by synthesizing insights from existing conceptual and empirical literature and adopted successful aging theory as a framework to the study. The study conceptualizes digital health as an enabling mechanism through which older adults can participate more actively in managing their health and maintaining social connectedness. In conclusion, disparities in digital access, privacy concerns, technological complexity, and age-related are key to the health benefits of the aging population. The study recommends a conceptual perspective that integrates technological, individual, and social factors to explain how digital health innovations can contribute to healthier, more autonomous, and socially connected ageing. items.title: Digital innovation and public acceptance of nuclear energy in the green transition
items.abstract: Public acceptance is widely regarded as a binding constraint on the contribution of nuclear energy to the green transition, yet claims that digital innovation will ease this constraint have rarely been examined against social science evidence. This topical review asks under what conditions digital innovation in nuclear energy systems, in particular digital twins, artificial intelligence (AI)-based predictive maintenance and the digitally supported design, manufacture and operation of small modular reactors (SMRs), can contribute to public acceptance of nuclear energy. The analysis draws on five strands of scholarship that are seldom brought into contact with the technical literature: risk perception research, cultural theory of risk, the deficit and engagement models of science communication, the social licence to operate, and socio-technical transitions theory, which serves as the integrating framework. Reading techno-optimistic claims through these lenses, the review identifies three structural barriers: a cybersecurity paradox, whereby the connectivity that enables digital safety functions simultaneously expands the attack surface; an economic gap, specific to SMRs, whereby projected cost reductions rest on serial-production assumptions that recent project experience has not supported; and a transparency fallacy, whereby information disclosure is expected to build trust although meta-analytic evidence links the benefit and risk perceptions associated with acceptance to trust rather than to knowledge. These barriers are argued to interact: cyber incidents could act as trust-destroying signal events, cost failures could undermine perceived institutional competence, and one-way transparency tools leave procedural justice concerns unaddressed. The review concludes that digital innovation is more likely to support acceptance when it is embedded in genuinely participatory engagement, when institutions demonstrably manage the new risks digitalisation creates, when economic claims are validated rather than promised, and when regulatory frameworks confer procedural legitimacy. Absent these conditions, digitalisation risks reproducing deficit-model assumptions that acceptance research has long found wanting.

items.title: Digital Policing and Artificial Intelligence: Implications for Community Trust and Police Legitimacy in Abia State, Nigeria
items.abstract: This study examines the implications of digital policing and Artificial Intelligence (AI) adoption in the Nigeria Police Force for community trust and police legitimacy, with particular reference to Abia State. Anchored in Procedural Justice Theory, the study adopts a qualitative desk-review design, synthesizing peer-reviewed literature on digital policing, algorithmic decision-making, and Nigerian police-community relations. Abia State, with a 2006 census population of 2,845,380 spread across seventeen local government areas, provides a densely populated, predominantly urban and semi-urban context in which the legitimacy consequences of digital policing carry direct relevance for millions of residents. The review finds that digital tools carry real potential to strengthen policing capacity, but that their value for legitimacy depends less on technical sophistication than on whether their deployment is experienced by citizens as fair, transparent, and respectful. Evidence from Nigerian policing scholarship indicates that public confidence in the police remains persistently low, human discretion continues to compromise the neutrality of ostensibly objective digital systems, and police-public digital interaction in Nigeria remains predominantly one-directional rather than participatory. The study argues that without deliberate attention to voice, neutrality, and trustworthiness, the introduction of AI and digital infrastructure into Nigerian policing risks reproducing, rather than resolving, the legitimacy deficits that have long characterized police-community relations, and recommends that digital policing reform in Abia State be paired with institutional accountability and genuine community engagement. Keywords: Digital policing, digitalization, artificial intelligence, police legitimacy, community trust, procedural justice, Abia State
